title: The AI Paradox: Why I'm Using Tech to Get Back to Paper
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: Emanuele presents a counter-intuitive conclusion from months of building custom AI Gems: the most advanced pedagogical move can be to reach for a pen and a visualiser instead of a laptop. Because time is a teacher's most precious currency, if a paper-and-visualiser question achieves the same impact in ten seconds, spending five minutes perfecting a digital slide is wasteful. He grounds the "low-tech" choice in Rosenshine's fourth principle (Provide Models): live modelling at a human pace, on the same medium students use, reduces cognitive load. His Ultra-Fast Hybrid Workflow assigns AI the "brawn" (atomisation drafts, worksheets, HTML) and reserves teacher "brain" for live procedural modelling.
points: After perfecting AI prompts, Emanuele deliberately tries to use his AI Gems as little as possible, a paradox rooted in the value of time.
Time is the teacher's most precious currency: if a paper question under a visualiser matches a slide's impact in seconds, the low-tech option wins.
Live modelling on paper (Rosenshine's 4th principle, Provide Models) is more effective than pre-baked animations because students see the process unfold at a human pace, reducing cognitive load.
His hybrid workflow lets AI handle atomisation drafts, lesson-cycle mapping, and worksheet/HTML generation while the teacher curates and models live.
Procedural skills (like placing tracing paper for rotations) are taught with a visualiser, not slides, so students see exactly how it is done.
quotes: Time is our most precious currency. Using AI saves time, but it still takes some time. If I can achieve the same pedagogical impact by writing a question on a piece of paper under a visualiser in 10 seconds, why would I spend 5 minutes perfecting a digital slide?

Research (specifically Rosenshine’s 4th Principle: Provide Models) suggests that watching a teacher think through a problem in real-time, on the same medium the students are using (paper), is far more effective than clicking through pre-baked animations
I treat the AI as a “Teaching Assistant” who has provided a first draft.
Use the tech. Use the AI. But don’t let it become another “job.
Sometimes, the most “advanced” thing you can do for your students is to pick up a pen, look them in the eye, and model the thinking process live.
